prompt: Does a plain SELECT under MVCC lock the rows it reads in Postgres?

options.text: Yes, an exclusive row lock until commit
Yes, a shared lock that blocks writers
No, plain SELECTs take no row locks
Only rows it reads through an index

explanation: Under MVCC a plain SELECT reads a snapshot and takes no row locks, which is why read-then-write isn't protected without FOR UPDATE, an atomic UPDATE or a version check. (a) and (b) describe FOR UPDATE and FOR SHARE, which you must ask for. (d) The access path doesn't change locking.

prompt: What does SELECT … FOR UPDATE do?

options.text: Applies the update immediately as it reads each row
Locks the selected rows; other lockers wait until commit
Locks the whole table so no other query can read it
Marks the rows so concurrent writes fail on commit

explanation: It takes row locks up front, so other transactions that try to lock or update those rows wait until you commit, making read-check-write safe. (a) It only reads; you still run the UPDATE. (c) It locks rows, not the table, and plain readers aren't blocked. (d) describes optimistic conflict detection, not FOR UPDATE.

prompt: Which Postgres clause lets each worker grab the next unlocked job without waiting?

options.text: NOWAIT
SKIP LOCKED
FOR SHARE
FOR NO KEY UPDATE

explanation: SKIP LOCKED skips rows other transactions hold, so each worker gets a different job without waiting. (a) NOWAIT errors instead of skipping. (c) and (d) are lock strengths; on their own they still wait for a locked row.

prompt: What's the best way to raise throughput?
scenario: A flash sale decrements one inventory row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Each transaction holds the lock for 5 ms. Sales cap at about 200 a second, even with 40 app servers.

options.text: Add more app servers so more sales run in parallel
Split stock into bucket rows to remove the hot row
Drop to Read Uncommitted so reads skip the lock
Raise lock_timeout so fewer waiting sales give up

explanation: One row lock held 5 ms caps you at about 200 per second whatever the server count. Splitting stock into bucket rows (or an atomic conditional UPDATE that holds the lock only briefly) removes the single hot row. (a) More servers just queue more. (c) Postgres treats Read Uncommitted as Read Committed, and writers still lock. (d) A longer timeout means longer queues, not more throughput.

prompt: In optimistic locking, how does a write detect a conflict?

options.text: It takes a lock first and waits if another writer has it
UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = ? changes 0 rows
The database raises a deadlock error on the second write
It re-reads the row after writing and compares the values

explanation: The UPDATE matches on the version it read; if someone else committed first, the version changed and 0 rows are updated. (a) describes pessimistic locking. (c) A version mismatch isn't a deadlock. (d) Re-reading after the write is too late: the other change has already been overwritten.

scenario: A wiki lets users edit a page for up to 20 minutes before saving. Two people editing the same page at once is rare but happens.

options.text: SELECT … FOR UPDATE held on the page while the user edits
A version column; on conflict, show a merge screen
Last write wins; conflicts are rare enough to ignore
A table lock taken when a user opens any page to edit

explanation: Never hold database locks over user think-time; conflicts are rare, so optimistic locking with a merge screen fits. (a) holds a lock and a connection for up to 20 minutes. (c) silently loses one person's edits when it does happen. (d) blocks every other editor on the whole wiki.

scenario: 300 concurrent requests update one counter row with optimistic version checks and retry on conflict. CPU is at 100% and fewer than 5% of attempts succeed.

options.text: High contention: most writes fail the version check and retry
Deadlocks: the retries lock rows in a different order each time
Lock waits: each retry queues behind a row lock held by others
A missing index on version makes each UPDATE scan the table

explanation: With hundreds of writers on one row, nearly every attempt fails the version check and retries, burning CPU. Pessimistic locking or removing the hot row works better. (b) Optimistic writes on one row don't form lock cycles. (c) Optimistic locking doesn't hold locks across the read; the waste is retries, not waits. (d) The UPDATE finds the row by id; version is just an extra condition.

prompt: What's the most effective way to prevent deadlocks in transfers between accounts?

options.text: Keep each transfer in a longer transaction
Always lock accounts in a consistent order
Lock each account with NOWAIT, never retry
Raise the deadlock_timeout to a few seconds

explanation: If every transfer locks the lower account ID first, two transfers can't each hold what the other needs, so no cycle forms. (a) Longer transactions make overlaps more likely. (c) NOWAIT turns waits into errors, and not retrying fails real transfers. (d) A longer timeout only delays detection; the deadlock still happens.

prompt: What does PostgreSQL do when it detects a deadlock?

options.text: Waits until lock_timeout ends both
Aborts one transaction with an error
Lets the older transaction go first
Rolls back both and retries them

explanation: Postgres picks a victim and aborts it with a deadlock error; the application must retry it. (a) Deadlock detection fires without any lock_timeout. (c) It doesn't reorder waits; a cycle can't be resolved without aborting someone. (d) It aborts only one, and never retries for you.

prompt: Why does a distributed lock need a fencing token?

options.text: So holders can renew the lease without asking the lock service
So storage rejects writes from a holder whose lease expired
So two clients can't acquire the lock at the same instant
So the lock service can tell which holder crashed and why

explanation: A process paused by GC or the network may still believe it holds the lock after its lease expired; an increasing token lets storage reject its stale writes. (a) Renewal still goes through the lock service. (c) Mutual exclusion at acquire time is the lock service's job; fencing protects against holders acting late. (d) Tokens don't diagnose crashes.
